basic_info.name: Qwen3 small models
basic_info.description: Alibaba's Qwen3 family of open-weight dense and Mixture-of-Experts causal language models, released under Apache-2.0, spanning 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B, 14B and 32B dense sizes plus 30B-A3B and 235B-A22B MoE variants. Trained on roughly 36 trillion tokens covering 119 languages and dialects including Hindi, and unified thinking and non-thinking modes in a single model. The small dense variants (1.7B and 4B) are the practical candidate for an offline, CPU-only health kiosk via llama.cpp GGUF quantization, and are the most credible local engine for constrained slot extraction plus a phase-2 narrative summary lane.
source_urls: https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3 (official repository, Apache-2.0, model family and license statement)
https://qwenlm.github.io/blog/qwen3/ (Qwen3 launch blog, 2025-04-29, dense model table and 119-language list)
https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B (1.7B model card, 28 layers, 16/8 GQA, 32K context)
https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B (4B model card, 36 layers, 32/8 GQA, 32K native / 131K with YaRN)
https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09388v1 (Qwen3 Technical Report, 0.6B-235B, thinking budget mechanism)
https://huggingface.co/b4ph/qwen3-4b-lowram-bench (reproducible CPU-only llama.cpp quantization ladder benchmark, Qwen3-4B)
https://huggingface.co/Arm/qwen3-1-7b-base-q4-k-m-llamacpp-vivo-x300 (Arm-optimized Q4_K_M measurement, 34.11 tok/s decode, 1127.98 MB, MMLU 61.05%)

technical_features.what_it_does: General-purpose text understanding and generation. For MediKiosk Module C the relevant use is constrained natural-language understanding - mapping elicited patient utterances and document extracts into structured slot values - and, only in a phase-2 lane, generating a narrative summary from already-structured fields. Qwen3 supports switching between a thinking mode for multi-step reasoning and a non-thinking mode for fast general chat within the same weights, plus a thinking-budget control that lets the caller cap reasoning effort at inference time.
technical_features.architecture: Decoder-only causal transformer. Dense variants: Qwen3-0.6B (28 layers), 1.7B (28 layers), 4B (36 layers), 8B (36 layers), 14B (40 layers), 32B (64 layers). Grouped-query attention throughout (1.7B uses 16 query / 8 KV heads; 4B uses 32 query / 8 KV heads). Tied embeddings on 0.6B/1.7B/4B. Native 32K context on the small dense models, 128K on 8B and above (4B reaches 131,072 tokens with YaRN). MoE variants are 30B-A3B (3B active) and 235B-A22B (22B active). Pretraining data was substantially enlarged versus Qwen2.5 (36T tokens vs 18T), with PDF-like documents text-extracted using Qwen2.5-VL and refined by Qwen2.5.
technical_features.inputs: Text prompts. No native structured-input schema; structured JSON output is obtained by prompting and/or grammar-constrained decoding in the serving runtime rather than by a built-in schema engine.
technical_features.outputs: Free text, or JSON-shaped text when constrained by prompt or grammar. For Module C the emitted FHIR/JSON must still be validated externally - the model does not itself guarantee FHIR R4 or NRCeS profile conformance.
technical_features.standards_compliance: None for clinical interoperability. Qwen3 carries no FHIR R4/R5 conformance, no NRCeS ABDM profile support, no SNOMED CT / LOINC / ICD binding and no clinical-terminology guarantees. Any OPConsultRecord or DocumentBundle conformance in the MediKiosk pipeline comes from the deterministic emitter and profile validation layer, not from this model. Qwen3 should be positioned as a text engine that feeds a conformance-checked emitter, never as the conformance mechanism.
technical_features.offline_capability: Full offline capability - the small dense variants run entirely on-device with no network dependency once weights are present, distributed as GGUF and executed by llama.cpp with CPU backends (ggml CPU_REPACK). This is the property that makes it viable for an offline-first kiosk, but it must co-reside with the ASR and OCR stacks inside the memory budget.
technical_features.languages_supported: 119 languages and dialects, up from 29 in Qwen2.5. The Indo-European block explicitly includes Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali, Oriya (Odia), Gujarati, Marathi, Nepali, Urdu, Assamese, Sindhi, Sinhala, Awadhi, Maithili, Bhojpuri, Magahi, Chhattisgarhi and Eastern Yiddish. Dravidian coverage includes Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam. Devanagari script languages are therefore well represented, but code-mixed Romanized Hinglish is not a first-class training category and needs the same prompt-level handling already planned for Module A.
technical_features.deployment_model: On-device / self-hosted. Runs on CPU via llama.cpp or ggml (also CUDA, Vulkan and other backends), on servers via vLLM or Transformers, and on mobile CPU with vendor-optimized builds (Arm SME2). No vendor cloud requirement, which satisfies the India data-residency constraint.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: Qwen3 dense base models match Qwen2.5 models with roughly double the parameters - Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B/14B/32B-Base perform comparably to Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B/72B-Base respectively, and outperform them on over half of benchmarks, especially STEM and coding. Quantization quality on Qwen3-4B (WikiText-2 perplexity, context 2048, CPU-only): F16 13.4304 baseline; Q8_0 13.4409 (+0.0105, effectively lossless); Q6_K 13.4404 (+0.0099); Q5_K_M 13.5362 (+0.1058); Q4_K_M 13.7304 (+0.3000); Q4_K_M+imatrix 13.6760 (+0.2456); Q3_K_M 15.6641 (+2.2337, a real quality cliff); Q3_K_M+imatrix 14.8237. Arm's optimized Qwen3-1.7B Q4_K_M measured MMLU 61.05% versus a 61.23% bf16 baseline on the same device.
performance_metrics.latency: CPU-only, no GPU offload (-ngl 0). Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M on a 16-core x86-64 CPU (AVX-512 + VNNI): 2064.8 t/s prompt processing at pp512 and 6.50 t/s generation at tg128; Q8_0 5.04 t/s, Q6_K 5.93 t/s, Q5_K_M 5.64 t/s, Q3_K_M 6.56 t/s generation. Qwen3-1.7B Q4_K_M on a mobile Arm CPU (vivo X300, 4 threads, 128-token prompt and 128 generated tokens): 34.11 tok/s decode and 809.12 ms time to first token, versus 2.77 tok/s and 34330 ms unoptimized. Practical implication: at roughly 6.5 t/s generation on a desktop-class CPU, a 200-token narrative summary costs on the order of 30 seconds of pure generation, which does not fit a 2-5 minute OPD slot when ASR and OCR also need the CPU.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M occupies a 2.50 GB file and runs in roughly 3 GB RAM; Q8_0 is 4.28 GB, Q6_K 3.31 GB, Q5_K_M 2.89 GB, Q3_K_M 2.08 GB, F16 8.05 GB. Qwen3-1.7B Q4_K_M measured 1127.98 MB with 2311.20 MB peak memory on the Arm reference device. Qwen3-0.6B Q4_K_M is 462 MB (Q5_K_M 526 MB, Q8_0 767 MB, FP16 1.4 GB), with approximate CPU throughput of 15-20 tok/s on 2 cores and 40-60 tok/s on 8 cores. On a ~4 GB kiosk the 4B Q4_K_M variant is a tight fit once the OS, ASR and OCR stages are resident, and concurrent execution of ASR, OCR and LLM is not viable.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: [uncertain] - no per-model download, deployment or call-volume figures were located for the Qwen3 small dense variants specifically. Family-level adoption exists for the wider Qwen series but was not verified at the granularity needed here.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Quality is measured by the vendor through standard academic benchmarks (MMLU, Multi-IF, INCLUDE, MMMLU, MT-AIME2024, PolyMath, MlogiQA) plus the published Qwen3 Technical Report. The quantization figures come from an independent, reproducible third-party harness: WikiText-2 perplexity via llama-perplexity (fixed corpus, context 2048, 16 threads, -ngl 0, seed 1) and throughput via llama-bench (pp512 / tg128, 5 repeats, mean), pinned to llama.cpp build 10516 commit b95502ba9. Arm's figures are vendor-measured but on a documented reference device with stated thread count, thermal state and warm-up protocol. No clinical or note-generation benchmark exists for this model, so clinical fitness remains untested.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: Qwen3 small dense models are the strongest current Apache-2.0 candidate to be the offline intelligence in Module C without any cloud dependency, which is the constraint that separates MediKiosk from the cloud-LLM competing approach. Two roles are plausible: (1) constrained NLU that maps elicited answers and digitized document text into the HistoryBundle slot schema, and (2) a phase-2 narrative summary lane consumed only after the deterministic renderer. The 1.7B Q4_K_M variant is the size that realistically fits a ~4 GB CPU-only kiosk alongside the rest of the stack. The quantization and CPU-throughput evidence found this sweep also gives Module C a defensible, citable performance floor instead of a guess.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: Qwen3-1.7B Q4_K_M (or Q5_K_M) as the constrained-NLU engine, chosen on the CPU latency and memory line where 4B is too close to the kiosk ceiling; the thinking-budget control to explicitly disable or minimize reasoning at inference. Consider for phase 2 only: a 4B-class model for narrative generation, gated behind the eval harness and only if the deterministic renderer is judged insufficient. Reject: thinking mode for note generation - reasoning traces demonstrably hurt note fidelity per arXiv:2605.24902 - and reject treating the model as any kind of conformance or grounding layer for FHIR output.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: Throughput is the binding constraint, not quality: ~6.5 t/s generation on a desktop-class 16-core CPU means a full narrative summary is tens of seconds, and on real kiosk-class ARM/i3 hardware it will be slower still, so the LLM lane must never sit on the critical path of a 2-5 minute consultation. Memory is the second constraint: 2.5-3 GB for Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M leaves little headroom on a ~4 GB machine shared with ASR and OCR, so serial scheduling with a watchdog is mandatory. The model has no clinical grounding, no terminology binding and no hallucination guardrail of its own, so a narrative lane reintroduces exactly the fabrication risk that motivated the deterministic-renderer decision. Code-mixed Hinglish is not a first-class training category, so Romanized input quality is unverified. All benchmark numbers are text-only and non-clinical, and none were measured on real Indian OPD kiosk hardware.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: Qwen3 strengthens the offline and data-residency differentiation because it removes the cloud-LLM dependency that the competing SIH approach carries, and it does so under a clean Apache-2.0 license. It does not, however, create differentiation on its own - any team can run a local Qwen3. MediKiosk's moat remains the deterministic, provenance-carrying renderer and NRCeS-conformant emission; Qwen3 is only permissible as an upstream understanding aid or a gated phase-2 narrative lane where every output is still traceable to a structured field.

business_info.license: Apache-2.0 for all open-weight Qwen3 models, confirmed in the official repository's license statement and in the individual Hugging Face model repositories. Permissive for commercial use with no copyleft or revenue-threshold clause, which is the decisive advantage over surya/marker weights (OpenRAIL-M) and other non-permissive candidates reviewed for this project.
business_info.pricing: Free - weights are open and downloadable at no cost. Any cost is self-hosted compute, not licensing.
business_info.funding: [uncertain] - Qwen is developed by Alibaba Group's Qwen Team and is corporate-funded rather than venture-funded; no discrete funding figure is applicable or was located.
business_info.commercial_status: Open-weight models released for unrestricted use under Apache-2.0, backed by a large commercial parent and an active open-source community.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: The local small-model field it competes with on a kiosk: Llama 3.x small variants, Google Gemma 3/Gemma 4 edge variants (the family a competing offline ABDM project chose), Phi small models, Mistral small models, and DeepSeek small distillations. On the evidence found this sweep, Qwen3's combination of Apache-2.0, 119 languages with strong Devanagari coverage, and a mature llama.cpp GGUF ecosystem is the strongest fit for this specific constraint set.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: llama.cpp and ggml (CPU, plus CUDA/Vulkan), Ollama, vLLM, Hugging Face Transformers, llama-cpp-python, and vendor-optimized mobile runtimes such as Arm SME2 builds. Quantized GGUF artifacts are published by both the vendor and a broad community, which lowers integration risk.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: The GGUF quantization ecosystem around Qwen3 is mature and independently benchmarked, including published importance-matrix recipes and reproducible CPU-only quantization-ladder results, which means MediKiosk can cite third-party performance evidence rather than vendor claims. Note that a newer generation (Qwen3.5, and Qwen3-2507 refreshes) is already appearing in the ecosystem, so a final engine pin should be re-checked against the newest compatible variant before the Module C design is frozen.

history.release_date: 2025-04-29 (initial Qwen3 family release, including the dense 1.7B and 4B models).
key_milestones: 2025-04-29 - Qwen3 launched: dense 0.6B/1.7B/4B/8B/14B/32B plus MoE 30B-A3B and 235B-A22B, all Apache-2.0, with unified thinking and non-thinking modes.
Qwen3 Technical Report published (arXiv:2505.09388) documenting the 0.6B-235B range, the thinking-budget mechanism and the expansion from 29 to 119 languages.
Qwen3-2507 refresh - updated Qwen3-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3-Thinking-2507 variants across 235B-A22B, 30B-A3B and 4B.
Arm-optimized GGUF releases for the small variants targeting mobile CPU with SME2, with published MMLU and throughput results.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: Movement in the last six months is concentrated on the small and edge end plus a generation refresh rather than on the original launch weights. The Qwen3-2507 update refreshed the Instruct and Thinking variants for 235B-A22B, 30B-A3B and 4B. Vendor-optimized GGUF builds for Qwen3-1.7B and a Qwen3.5-2B variant were published with measured mobile-CPU throughput, MMLU accuracy, file size and peak memory, giving current, reproducible CPU figures where none previously existed for this class. A Qwen3.5 generation is now visible in the ecosystem. The core 1.7B and 4B cards continue to document 32K context, 119 languages and Apache-2.0 licensing, so the selection basis is unchanged; the practical action is to pin a specific quantized artifact and re-check the newest compatible variant before freezing the Module C engine decision.

market_positioning.target_users: Developers and organizations deploying self-hosted or on-device language models, including edge, privacy-sensitive and offline deployments.
market_positioning.market_segment: Open-weight local / on-device large language models, positioned as a permissive-license alternative to Llama and Gemma for multilingual and resource-constrained deployments.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: Alibaba positions Qwen3 as its most advanced open model family to date, offering dense and MoE sizes from 0.6B to 235B, unified thinking and non-thinking modes with adaptive thinking budgets, and support for 119 languages and dialects - all open-weight under Apache-2.0.
